title: How do you lead a case by proposing the next step?
description: Interviewers score whether you drive. Waiting to be told what to do loses candidate-led cases. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Lead the case by ending every answer with a proposal: what you found, why it matters for the goal, what you want to look at next and the data you need for it. Choose the next step that best tests your leading explanation, and summarise in two lines whenever you finish a branch. If the interviewer redirects you, follow them without fuss.
body:
Stage 5 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why leading matters

Interviewers want to see whether you can run a problem, not just answer questions about it. A candidate who finishes every answer with "Where would you like me to go next?" is handing the work back. In candidate-led cases that can sink you. In interviewer-led cases, which are common at McKinsey, the interviewer picks the next question anyway, but saying where you would go and why still shows the judgement they are looking for. The longer version of this stage is in how to drive a case.

The four-part move

After your structure and after every answer, say four things:

  1. Finding: what the data shows.
  2. So what: what it means for the client's goal.
  3. Next step: what you want to look at, and why.
  4. Data request: the specific information you need.
"So higher delivery-app commissions explain most of the margin drop. As a next step I'd like to see profit per order by channel, to test whether delivery orders make money after commission. Do we have that?"

How to choose the next step

When several next steps are possible, pick the one that best tests your leading explanation. Three questions help you choose:

  • Which branch is biggest? Go where most of the money is.
  • Which explanation is most likely? Test your hypothesis first.
  • Which test is quickest? If two branches are equal, start with the one a single number can settle.

A worked example

A retailer's revenue has fallen from $50M to $45M. You learn that its average price per transaction is unchanged at $25. So transactions must have fallen from 2.0M ($50M ÷ $25) to 1.8M ($45M ÷ $25), a 10% drop.

Weak: "Price is flat. What would you like me to look at next?"
Strong: "Price is unchanged, so the whole decline is volume: transactions are down 10%, from 2.0M to 1.8M. I want to split that between fewer customers and fewer purchases per customer, because the fixes are very different. Do we have those figures?"

Suppose the data shows customers fell from 400k to 360k while each still buys five times a year: 360k × 5 = 1.8M. The entire drop is lost customers. Your next proposal follows naturally:

"So we've lost 10% of our customers, and the ones who stayed are buying as often as before. Next I'd like to know where they went. Did a competitor open nearby, or did we close or change anything? Do we have customer numbers by store?"

Each step narrows the problem. That is what leading looks like.

Summarise at the turns

When you finish one bucket of your structure, summarise in two lines and steer to the next:

"Let me quickly summarise where we are. We know the market is attractive and our product can compete. The open question is whether the economics work, so I'd like to look at the investment needed."

Mini-summaries keep the interviewer with you, keep you oriented and give you the bones of your final recommendation.

When the interviewer has a different plan

Sometimes you propose one thing and the interviewer says, "Let's look at costs instead." That is normal, especially in interviewer-led cases. Say "Sure" and move on. You have already shown your reasoning, and arguing for your sequence wastes time and goodwill. The aim is to show logical sequencing while staying collaborative, not to take over the conversation.

If you get stuck and cannot see the next step, step back out loud: "We know A and B, and we're trying to get to X, so the next thing to check is C."

Common mistakes

  • Ending with "Where should I go next?" Replace it with a proposal.
  • Proposing without a reason. "Next I'd look at costs" is weaker than "Next I'd look at costs, because revenue is flat, so the profit fall must come from there."
  • Asking for "all the data". Ask for the specific number that tests your idea.
  • Moving on without a summary. Close each branch before opening the next.
  • Pushing back on a redirect. Follow the interviewer's lead gracefully.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. You have just answered a question about costs. Keep driving the case.

Show a strong answer

"So higher delivery-app commissions explain most of the margin drop. As a next step I'd like to see profit per order by channel, to test whether delivery orders make money after commission. Do we have that?"

Why it works: Finding, next step, data needed, and why.

2. You have covered two of your three buckets. Summarise and steer.

Show a strong answer

"Let me quickly summarise where we are: the market is attractive and our product can compete. The open question is whether the economics work, so I'd like to look at the investment needed."

Why it works: It closes what is done and opens the last branch with a reason.

3. An airline's profit fell. You have found that revenue per passenger is flat but passenger numbers fell 8%. What do you propose?

Show a strong answer

"So the problem is volume, not price. I'd like to see passengers by route, to check whether the drop is spread across the network or concentrated on a few routes, perhaps where a competitor has added flights. Do we have route-level data?"

Why it works: It names the finding, a likely explanation and the one cut of the data that would test it.

Where to practise next

Pick a case from the casebook and practise only the transitions: after each question, say your four-part move before reading the next one. Drill the lines on the perfect casing page, and read the next stage, what to say when you are handed a chart.
